title: Log every prompt and completion from day one
linkedin_md:
# Log every prompt and completion from day one

If your LLM product can change behavior without a deploy, you need a record of what it did. Not a sampled subset. Not just status codes. The prompt and completion are the executable trace.

Most teams start with a thin log: request id, model name, latency, token counts. That is enough to bill and alert, not enough to debug. When a user says the assistant gave a wrong answer, you need the exact rendered prompt, the system instructions, the retrieved context, the tool calls, the sampling settings, and the raw completion.

What to log:
- request id, timestamp, user id hashed or pseudonymized
- model name and version, provider region if relevant
- full rendered messages, including system, user, assistant, tool messages
- retrieval context or tool outputs fed into the prompt
- sampling parameters: temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences
- completion text, tool calls, structured output, finish reason
- token counts, cost estimate, latency, retry count, error class
- experiment or prompt version tags

[YOUR STORY HERE - 2-3 paragraphs]

The cost is usually manageable. Say you serve 10,000 requests per day. If the average prompt is 1,500 tokens and completion is 500 tokens, that is 20 million tokens per day, or 600 million per month. Raw text might be a few megabytes per 1,000 requests, so a month of logs could be tens of gigabytes. At $0.02 per GB per month, 100 GB is $2 before query costs. Object storage plus a queryable index is cheap compared with a week of engineers reconstructing incidents from memory.

The bigger risk is not storage. It is uncontrolled access. Log every prompt and completion, but put them behind role based access, encryption, retention rules, and audit trails. For regulated data, keep the payload encrypted at rest and restrict plaintext access to incident response. Do not put secrets in prompts unless you are ready to store them.

Why full logs matter:

## The prompt is the code

With LLMs, behavior is not only in your code. It is in the prompt. A one word change in a system message can move accuracy by several points, break tool calling, or create a new failure mode. If you only log a version id, you still cannot answer what the model saw.

Rendered prompt logs give you a replay. You can take yesterday's request, call the same model version with the same parameters, and see whether the failure persists. That turns "it feels worse" into a reproducible case.

## Completions are the eval set

You cannot build good evals from synthetic prompts alone. Real completions are the best source of edge cases. A small team can review 200 completions per week and still find the top failure modes: refusal loops, tool hallucination, truncated JSON, leaked context, wrong language, overconfident answers.

Store completions in a pipeline that can be filtered by model, prompt version, user segment, tool, or error type. That lets you compare before and after. Without that, you ship prompt changes on intuition.

## Incidents need timelines

When an outage happens, you need to know whether it was model behavior, retrieval quality, tool failure, prompt drift, or a provider issue. Full logs let you slice by minute and request. You can see that a bad answer began after a retrieval index update, not after a model switch.

This is where a sampled log fails. The user report may be the only instance that matters, and you did not keep it.

[YOUR STORY HERE - 2-3 paragraphs]

## Takeaways

- Log the rendered prompt, not just a template version.
- Store the raw completion, tool calls, finish reason, and errors.
- Add request id, model version, prompt version, and sampling parameters to every record.
- Keep full payloads for 30 to 90 days if you need debugging depth.
- Put logs behind access control, encryption, retention, and deletion paths.
- Use real completions as eval fixtures and regression tests.
- Build replay before the first incident.

The goal is not a giant observability platform. The goal is a boring, reliable record of what your system said and why. If you cannot replay it, you cannot fix it.
